As artificial intelligence creates some of the fastest-growing and most-lucrative jobs globally, women are underrepresented in roles from the C-suite to rank-and-file positions at AI companies, according to a new analysis published August 18, 2026.

## The Growing Gender Gap

The AI industry is generating some of the highest-paying jobs in the technology sector, with average salaries for AI engineers surpassing $200,000 in major markets. However, women account for only about 22% of the global AI workforce, according to recent Interface EU research. This number drops further up the corporate ladder—women hold less than 14% of senior executive roles in AI companies.

The disparity extends beyond leadership positions. At the rank-and-file level, women are significantly underrepresented in technical AI roles, including machine learning engineering, data science, and research positions. The gap has actually widened in recent years as the industry has scaled rapidly.

## Why It Matters

The exclusion of women from AI roles carries significant implications for both economic equity and technology development. With AI systems increasingly making decisions that affect billions of people, diverse teams are critical for reducing bias in algorithms. Research has consistently shown that homogeneous teams are more likely to embed systemic biases into AI systems.

"It's a $5 trillion opportunity that the industry keeps leaving on the table," noted one industry researcher. "We're building the most transformative technology of our generation with only half the population fully参与."

## International Context

The International Labour Organization has confirmed that women face higher workplace risks from generative AI compared to men. While AI is expected to drive job growth in technology-intensive sectors, women remain largely excluded from these opportunities. Globally, women accounted for only about 30% of the AI workforce in 2022—only 4 percentage points higher than in 2016, showing minimal progress.

The World Economic Forum has warned that generative AI is reshaping jobs but widening gender gaps. Women face more disruption and less opportunity from AI automation, and urgent action is needed to ensure equity in the tech workforce.

## Industry Response

Some AI companies have begun implementing targeted programs to increase female representation, including mentorship initiatives, scholarship programs, and biased hiring practice audits. However, advocates say the pace of change remains insufficient to close the gap by 2030.
